title: Chili con carne
subtitle: Texas-influenced beef and chilli stew
excerpt: Diced chuck beef braised slowly with dried chillies, cumin, garlic, tomatoes, and beef stock until deeply flavoured and slightly thickened. Served with rice, sour cream, and pickled jalapeños. With beans on the side.
sourceNotes: Chili con carne has a complex origin spanning the borderland of Texas and Mexico from at least the mid-nineteenth century. It appears in U.S. documents from the 1880s and is documented in the Texas State Legislature's records of San Antonio's Chili Queens. It was standardised in various American home cooking texts from the late nineteenth century onwards including Fannie Farmer (1896, public domain) and in twentieth-century Tex-Mex cookbooks.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes excellently. Cool and freeze in portions. Defrost overnight and reheat gently with a splash of water or stock.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Better the next day.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make 1 to 2 days ahead for the best flavour.

content.text: This is not a quick chilli. Properly-made chili con carne uses diced beef chuck, not mince, and it cooks for 2 to 2.5 hours until the meat is tender and the sauce is thick and deeply flavoured. The debate about beans divides Texas from everywhere else: if you add them, add them at the end, or serve them on the side. The chilli is better without them in the pot.

items.prepNote: soaked in boiling water for 20 minutes, drained, seeded, finely chopped
chipotle chillies in adobo sauce, finely chopped

content.text: Season the beef generously with salt. Heat the oil in a large, heavy casserole over high heat. Brown the beef in batches, taking care not to crowd the pan. 3 to 4 minutes per batch. Lift out and set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Cook the onion for 8 minutes until soft. Add the garlic, dried chillies, chipotle, cumin, paprika, and oregano. Cook for 2 minutes, stirring, until fragrant.

Return the beef to the pot. Add the tomatoes and stock. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a low simmer. Cover and cook for 2 to 2.5 hours, stirring occasionally, until the beef is completely tender and the sauce has thickened. If the sauce is too loose, uncover for the last 30 minutes.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve with rice, sour cream, grated cheddar, and pickled jalapeños.

items.cause: Chipotle and ancho together are quite hot
items.fix: Use fewer chipotles. Add a teaspoon of sugar or a square of dark chocolate to balance the heat. Sour cream at the table is the classic fix.

items.symptom: Beef is still tough after 2.5 hours
items.cause: Chuck needs long, low heat; boiling rather than simmering toughens the fibres
items.fix: Ensure it is at a low simmer, not a boil. Give it another 30 minutes.

content.text: Chili con carne is the state dish of Texas. The 1977 Texas legislature act naming it the Official State Dish is still referenced in cookbooks. The debate about beans, tomatoes, and the correct cut of meat is fiercely contested and regional. Texans use diced beef, no beans, and as many dried chillies as possible. The rest of America uses mince and kidney beans. Both are right in their own contexts.
